needs_redesign.capability: Wearable Data Layer contract (WearDataContract): DataClient persistent paths, MessageClient transient paths, ChannelClient bulk paths, capability advertisement, and the `_ts` dedup-buster
needs_redesign.why: WatchConnectivity has no path-routed bus. It has four primitives with different delivery semantics and the mapping is not one-to-one: `updateApplicationContext` (single latest-value dictionary, replaces previous, background-delivered — the DataClient analogue), `transferUserInfo` (FIFO queue, guaranteed, survives app termination — no Android analogue, strictly better for alerts), `sendMessage` (requires `isReachable`, immediate — the MessageClient analogue), `transferFile` (bulk — the ChannelClient analogue, now only needed if anything bulk survives). Crucially there is only ONE application context per direction, so the eight distinct DataClient paths must be folded into one versioned dictionary or split across transports. Capability advertisement (`android_wear_capabilities`) has no analogue — `WCSession` exposes `isPaired` / `isWatchAppInstalled` / `isReachable` / `isComplicationEnabled` / `activationState` instead. And WidgetKit extensions CANNOT hold a `WCSession` — only the app can, so every wrist-side data arrival must wake the watch app, which then calls `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines`.
options: One versioned application context dictionary carrying all latest-value state (CGM, IoB, config, category labels, monitoring status, thresholds, unit) with a monotonic `seq`; `transferUserInfo` for alerts and history batches; `sendMessage` for dismiss and chat when reachable.
Keep the eight logical paths as top-level keys inside a single application-context dictionary, so the contract file and its tests port almost verbatim and only the transport layer under it changes.
Abandon latest-value semantics and put everything on `transferUserInfo`, gaining guaranteed ordered delivery at the cost of a queue that backs up while the watch is off-wrist.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Keep a single `WearContract.swift` in `GlycemicCore` with the same key names and the same contract test that pins every string — the value of that file was never the transport. Structure it as: (1) ONE application context dictionary with a monotonic `seq: Int64` plus nested sub-dictionaries keyed by the existing path names, carrying CGM, IoB, config, category labels, monitoring status and the glucose unit — latest-value-wins is exactly right for all of these and `updateApplicationContext` costs no budget; (2) `transferUserInfo` for alerts (guaranteed, FIFO, wakes the watch app in the background, survives watch app termination) and for the three history batches; (3) `sendMessage` for alert dismiss and any chat fallback, with `transferUserInfo` as the unreachable fallback; (4) `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` reserved exclusively for material complication changes (see the refresh-cadence item). KEEP the `_ts`/`seq` dedup-buster: `updateApplicationContext` is documented to replace the context but is not documented to redeliver an identical one, and a monotonic sequence number costs nothing and preserves the load-bearing heartbeat delivery. Keep the unit token on the CGM payload rather than the config payload, for the documented reason. Close the write-only status gap while porting: the phone must actually consume watch-side status replies rather than repeating the Story 32.4 TODO.

needs_redesign.capability: Phone→watch data streaming (WearDataSender) driven by PumpPollingOrchestrator's 15 s fast loop and 300 s slow loop inside a foreground service
needs_redesign.why: iOS has no foreground services and no reliable periodic timer. `PumpConnectionService` staying alive for hours is not reproducible. The only dependable wake source while a pump is connected is Core Bluetooth: with `bluetooth-central` in `UIBackgroundModes` plus `CBCentralManager` state restoration, iOS relaunches the app on peripheral notify/connect/disconnect and gives roughly 10 s of runtime (extendable to ~30 s with `beginBackgroundTask`). `BGAppRefreshTask`/`BGProcessingTask` are opportunistic — the system decides, commonly 15 min to hours apart, never at a guaranteed cadence, and NEVER after the user force-quits the app. So a 15 s fast loop cannot exist; the effective cadence is 'whenever the pump/CGM notifies', which for CGM is naturally ~5 min. Separately, wrist delivery is metered: `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` draws from a system daily budget (historically ~50/day, exposed at runtime via `WCSession.remainingComplicationUserInfoTransfers`), and 288 CGM readings/day cannot each buy a high-priority complication wake.
options: Push everything on every BLE wake and accept that the wrist complication only refreshes when budget allows.
Push the full state to `updateApplicationContext` on every BLE wake (free, no budget), and spend a `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` only on materially-changed renders.

Make the watchOS app fetch from the self-hosted backend itself via `WKURLSessionRefreshBackgroundTask`, so the wrist has a data path that does not depend on the phone at all (backend-connected mode only).
Drop the wrist complication refresh entirely and rely on Live Activities forwarded to the Smart Stack.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Layer three mechanisms. (1) On every Core Bluetooth wake, write the full latest state into `updateApplicationContext` — unmetered, background-delivered, and it also populates `receivedApplicationContext` for the watch's cold-start bootstrap. (2) Spend a metered `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` only when the render would MATERIALLY change: a glucose band crossing (per `bgColor`), a freshness-tier transition, an alert state change, or a coverage-state change — plus a floor of roughly one every 15 minutes. Budget the spend against `remainingComplicationUserInfoTransfers` and degrade to plain `transferUserInfo` when exhausted. (3) In backend-connected mode, additionally let the watch pull with `WKApplication.scheduleBackgroundRefresh` + `WKURLSessionRefreshBackgroundTask` (a few per hour, more when the app's complication is on the active face), which gives the wrist an independent data path and is the honest answer to 'the phone died'. Replace the swallow-everything error handling with a bounded outbound queue — `transferUserInfo` gives guaranteed FIFO delivery for free, which is strictly better than Android's 'a disconnected watch is a no-op'. And rethrow `CancellationError` uniformly (Swift's structured concurrency makes the three-old-methods-swallow-cancellation bug impossible if you use `try` correctly).

needs_redesign.capability: Watch-side data receipt & fan-out (GlycemicDataListenerService): two-pass ordering, per-path validation, and the throttled complication fan-out (BG 30 s, IoB 60 s, graph 15 s/120 s adaptive, alerts unthrottled, history immediate)
needs_redesign.why: `WearableListenerService` has no watchOS analogue — there is no background service that can be started by a data arrival. The receiver is `WCSessionDelegate` on the watch APP, which the system wakes in the background for `transferUserInfo` / `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` / application-context arrivals, and which then must call `WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines`. The two-pass ordering (config before data) becomes unnecessary for the application-context path — one dictionary arrives atomically — but is still needed across transports. More importantly, the Android throttle constants were tuned against CPU cost; on watchOS the constraint is a hard system reload budget, so 30 s/60 s/15 s reload floors would be blown through in under an hour and the system would silently stop honouring reloads. Finally, direct background vibration is not available: `WKInterfaceDevice.play(_:)` only works while the app is running in the foreground, so the alert haptic must become a notification.
options: Port the throttles as-is and discover the budget ceiling on device (Simulator does not enforce it).
Replace time-based reload throttles with change-significance gating plus pre-baked timeline entries for all time-driven transitions.
Keep a small on-watch scheduler that batches reload requests into at most N per hour, tracked in the App Group store.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Delete the time-based throttles and replace them with two mechanisms. First, PRE-BAKE every time-driven transition as timeline entries: when a CGM reading arrives, the timeline includes entries at now, ts+6 min, ts+15 min; when a monitoring status arrives, an entry at receivedAt+timeoutMs. That reproduces the entire GLY-116 axis-(b) and axis-(a) decay with zero reloads, which is what the Android UPDATE_PERIOD_SECONDS=300 was paying for. Second, call `reloadTimelines` only on MATERIAL change (band crossing, alert change, coverage change, history backfill) and keep alerts unthrottled as today. Port every per-path validation rule literally — the 0..500 count gate, the 15 U/hr and 25 U caps, the timeout clamp to 10 s..30 min, the VALID_MONITORING_STATES rejection, the `isValidGlucose` reject-the-whole-CGM-event rule, the apply-unit-before-validating rule, the `sanitizeThresholds` defaults 70/180/55/250, and `rebuzz` defaulting to true. Replace the `Vibrator` call with `UNUserNotificationCenter.add()` scheduled ON THE WATCH (see the alert delivery item).

needs_redesign.capability: Complication provider: alerts (bell) — the coverage-honesty glance, encoded entirely as a tint (grey / yellow / red) with a load-bearing six-branch precedence
needs_redesign.why: This is the single highest-risk item in the whole subsystem. watchOS complications render in an accented/tinted mode: the system applies the watch face's tint to your content and you can only split it into accented and non-accented groups via `.widgetAccentable()`. You cannot rely on arbitrary hue surviving — grey vs amber vs red, the entire encoding of the dead-phone cue, can be flattened to a single face-chosen colour. The Android design deliberately makes 'quiet grey bell' mean 'something is currently watching' and 'amber bell' mean 'coverage degraded or unknown, even with zero alerts'. If both render identically on the wrist, the port silently deletes the dead-phone cue in exactly the case it exists for.
options: Ship the bell with colour only and accept the flattening (unsafe — deletes the cue).

Re-encode the six branches on SHAPE and SYMBOL rather than hue: distinct SF Symbols per state (bell / bell.badge / bell.slash / exclamationmark.triangle.fill / questionmark.circle), plus a text badge, so the state is legible in monochrome.
Move the coverage cue off the complication onto a Live Activity forwarded to the Smart Stack, where more layout room and (in-app-style) colour are available.
Use `.accessoryRectangular` rather than `.accessoryCircular` so a short text state label ('watching' / 'not watching' / 'no recent data') can sit next to the glyph.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Re-encode on symbol + text, not colour. Provide `.accessoryCircular` (distinct SF Symbol per branch, `.widgetAccentable()` on the alarming states so they take the face accent) AND `.accessoryRectangular` (symbol plus a one-line state label carrying the same copy the AlertsActivity uses). Keep the pure six-branch `render(alert, coverage, nowMs)` function unchanged in `GlycemicCore` — only its output type changes from a tint Int to a (symbol, label, accentable) triple. Keep the precedence ordering exactly, including the load-bearing rule that the stale-alert quiet state may only render while coverage is Watching. Keep the full `contentDescription` strings as `.accessibilityLabel`, unchanged — VoiceOver is the one channel where the current copy survives verbatim, and for this app it is arguably the most important one. Add a colour-blind/monochrome review gate: the four states must be distinguishable in a greyscale screenshot.

needs_redesign.capability: Complication provider: glucose graph (400×100 ARGB bitmap sparkline, 7-layer draw order, per-segment glucose colouring, basal/IoB/mode-band overlays, hash-based bitmap cache)
needs_redesign.why: Three separate problems. (1) The output is a fixed 400×100 bitmap sized for a WFF `PartImage` slot; watchOS accessory families are system-sized and the app never controls the geometry. (2) The accessory rendering mode flattens colour, so per-segment red/yellow/green glucose banding, the purple/orange mode bands, the teal/blue-grey basal colouring and the blue IoB overlay all collapse — the overlay system is *entirely* colour-encoded. (3) `.accessoryCircular` is far too small for a 3-hour sparkline with four overlay layers, and even `.accessoryRectangular` is a narrow strip.
options: Draw with SwiftUI `Canvas` in `.accessoryRectangular` only, dropping all overlays and keeping a single monochrome glucose line with target-band shading via opacity.
Keep the overlays but differentiate by opacity/line style/dash pattern instead of hue.
Put the rich multi-overlay graph only in the watch app detail screen and the iPhone Home Screen widget (both full colour) and let the complication be a minimal trend strip.
Ship a `.accessoryCorner` gauge instead of a graph.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Split it. On the wrist complication, ship `.accessoryRectangular` with a SwiftUI `Canvas` sparkline: glucose line at full accent, target-range band as a low-opacity fill, threshold lines dashed, and NO basal/bolus/IoB/mode overlays — the Android code already hardcodes bolus markers off at 400×100 for exactly this 'too small' reason, and on a watchOS accessory strip the same argument extends to all four overlays. Put the full seven-layer, full-colour rendering in (a) the watch app's GraphDetailActivity equivalent and (b) an iPhone Home Screen widget, where `WidgetRenderingMode.fullColor` genuinely is available and the colour encoding survives intact. Drop the bitmap hash cache — SwiftUI `Canvas` re-renders per timeline entry with no bitmap to cache, and WidgetKit's own entry diffing covers it. Keep the MIN_READINGS=3 gate, the range-window cutoff, thresholds taken from the LAST reading in the window, and the 'x-axis spans first→last reading, not cutoff→now' behaviour. Fix the Y-clamp inconsistency (20/500 sparkline vs 40/400 detail) to one value in `GlycemicCore`.

needs_redesign.capability: Phone→watch monitoring-status mirror with a heartbeat (WearMonitoringStatusForwarder: re-send every max(timeoutMs/2, 5 s) — 3 min in production — from the pump service's scope, with retryWhen resubscribe)
needs_redesign.why: THE HEARTBEAT MECHANISM IS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE ON iOS. There is no guaranteed periodic wake: no foreground service, no AlarmManager-equivalent that runs arbitrary code, `BGAppRefreshTask` is opportunistic and typically far coarser than 3 minutes, and a force-quit app is never relaunched. The DESIGN INTENT, however, is not only implementable but is MORE necessary on iOS than on Android, because iOS has more ways for the phone to go silent (force-quit, BLE state-restoration not firing, Low Power Mode, the user revoking Bluetooth). The Android design uses arrival CADENCE to restart a watch-side timer; iOS must use an explicit DEADLINE instead, so that a phone that gets only sporadic wakes still advertises a coverage claim the watch can decay correctly.
options: Keep a cadence-based heartbeat and accept that it fires irregularly, over-decaying the wrist to 'no recent data' on a healthy phone.
Change the wire payload to advertise an absolute `validUntilMs` deadline alongside the state, so the watch's decay is anchored to a deadline the phone chose rather than to arrival timing.
Piggyback the coverage claim on every CGM/IoB push (which is BLE-driven and therefore naturally ~5-minutely while a pump is connected) instead of on an independent timer.
Have the watch derive coverage itself from data freshness — rejected, this breaks the documented 'the watch NEVER re-derives coverage' invariant.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Do options 2 and 3 together, and keep option 1 as a best-effort supplement. The monitoring-status payload gains an absolute `validUntilMs` computed by the phone as `now + timeoutMs`; the watch's `coverageFrom` decays against that deadline rather than against `receivedAt + timeoutMs`, so an irregular delivery cadence no longer produces false 'no recent data'. The claim rides along on EVERY application-context write — every BLE wake, every CGM reading, every IoB poll — so it is refreshed by the same event stream that proves the phone is alive, which is exactly what the heartbeat was proxying for. Additionally register a `BGAppRefreshTask` that re-advertises when the system grants one. Keep the wire vocabulary (`server_active`, `floor_watching`, `not_watching` plus the five verbatim reason names) and the contract test that pins it — this is a load-bearing contract. Keep the watch-side clamp of the advertised window to 10 s..30 min and the fail-closed rejection of unknown state strings. Keep monitoring status unpersisted. Explicitly accept and document the honesty hole iOS adds: a force-quit iPhone app will not be relaunched by Core Bluetooth, and the wrist's decay to 'no recent data' is the ONLY signal the user gets — which is precisely the behaviour this design already produces.

needs_redesign.capability: Alert delivery to the wrist: vibration fired directly by the watch service (waveform for urgent, one-shot for warning), gated on showAlert, with rebuzz defaulting to true
needs_redesign.why: watchOS has no API to trigger a haptic from the background — `WKInterfaceDevice.current().play(_:)` only works while the app is running and foreground. The supported way to alert the wrist is a notification. But mirroring an iPhone local notification to the watch is NOT guaranteed: iOS mirrors notifications to the watch only when the iPhone is locked/asleep and the watch is on-wrist and unlocked; if the iPhone is unlocked and in use, the alert stays on the phone and the wrist stays silent. Separately, breaking through Silent Mode, Focus, Do Not Disturb and Sleep Focus requires the `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts` entitlement, which Apple grants case-by-case on written request and is NOT available by simply ticking a box in Xcode.
options: Mirror an iPhone local notification and accept non-guaranteed wrist delivery.

Schedule the local notification ON THE WATCH itself, driven by a `transferUserInfo` that wakes the watch app in the background — guarantees wrist delivery independently of where the iPhone is or whether it is unlocked.
Deliver via APNs from the self-hosted backend (backend-connected mode only), which reaches the watch directly when it has its own network route.
Request the Critical Alerts entitlement and, if denied, fall back to Time Sensitive interruption level.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Schedule the alert notification ON THE WATCH. The phone sends the alert as a `transferUserInfo` (guaranteed FIFO, wakes the watch app in the background even when suspended), and the watch app calls `UNUserNotificationCenter.add()` with an immediate trigger. This is the only path that makes the wrist alert independent of iPhone lock state, and it is a genuine improvement over Android. Request the Critical Alerts entitlement for urgent_low / urgent_high with `UNNotificationSound.defaultCriticalSound`; enable the freely-available `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.time-sensitive` entitlement and use `.timeSensitive` interruption level for low/high, and as the fallback for urgent if Critical Alerts is denied. Port the 30-min re-buzz as a LOCALLY SCHEDULED ladder on the watch using `UNTimeIntervalNotificationTrigger` — these fire even when the app is suspended or terminated, so the wrist keeps re-alarming on an ongoing emergency even if the phone dies, which Android cannot do. Bound that ladder: it must terminate once the underlying reading ages past TOO_STALE, and the terminating notification must say the data is stale and nothing is currently watching, rather than continuing to re-buzz off a frozen snapshot. Keep the `showAlert` toggle (rename it honestly — 'Wrist alerts' — since on iOS it suppresses scheduling, and the system also gives the user independent control in Settings and the Watch app, which the UI must acknowledge). Keep `rebuzz` defaulting to true. Preserve the 5-min silent refresh that keeps the shown alert inside the 6-min STALE band — on iOS this rides the natural BLE CGM cadence.

needs_redesign.capability: Phone→watch alert relay state machine (PumpPollingOrchestrator): the isReadingAlertable data-trust gate, watchRelayMutex serialisation, NEW/ONGOING/RECOVERY transitions, WRIST_ALERT_REFRESH_MS 5 min, WRIST_ALERT_REBUZZ_MS 30 min
needs_redesign.why: The decision logic ports verbatim and MUST — 'never retract an alert on untrusted data' is the most safety-load-bearing rule in the subsystem. What changes is its host: there is no poll loop guaranteed to run, so the 5-minute silent refresh and the 30-minute re-buzz cannot be driven by 'the next iteration of the loop'. `watchRelayMutex` becomes a Swift `actor`, which is a straightforward improvement.
options: Drive transitions only from Core Bluetooth wakes and accept that a disconnected pump produces no refresh (which is arguably correct — no reading means no alertable reading).
Keep the phone as the sole scheduler and add a BGAppRefreshTask supplement.
Move the re-buzz ladder to the watch (scheduled local notifications) and keep only the state transitions on the phone.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Make the state machine an `actor` and drive it from Core Bluetooth reading arrivals, which is the natural ~5-min cadence while a pump is connected — this preserves WRIST_ALERT_REFRESH_MS 5 min exactly. Move the 30-minute re-buzz cadence to a watch-scheduled notification ladder (above), so an ongoing emergency keeps alarming the wrist even if the phone stops. Port `isReadingAlertable` and the rule that a non-alertable reading skips the WHOLE block — no send, no clear, latch untouched — with its comment intact. Port the rule that RECOVERY is keyed on the server CLASSIFICATION being null rather than on the watch-type mapping being null. Port `SERVER_TO_WATCH_ALERT_TYPE` and the 'a mapping gap may cost the watch relay, never the alert-floor hand-off' behaviour.

needs_redesign.capability: On-watch AI chat (ChatActivity: voice input, TTS with configured voice, markdown stripping, 30 s timeout) + phone relay (WearChatRelayService: foreground service blocking a binder thread for a 90 s LLM call)
needs_redesign.why: Three distinct platform breaks. (1) The relay's whole architecture — promote to a foreground service, then `runBlocking` on the binder thread so GMS does not unbind before the LLM answers — is meaningless on iOS: there are no foreground services and `WCSession.sendMessage`'s reply handler times out in tens of seconds, far short of the 90 s API budget. (2) `SFSpeechRecognizer` (the Speech framework) is NOT available on watchOS; `RecognizerIntent.ACTION_RECOGNIZE_SPEECH` has no direct equivalent. (3) `AVSpeechSynthesizer` IS available on watchOS, so TTS ports, but audio session handling and background audio on watchOS are restricted.
options: Keep a phone relay and use `transferUserInfo` request + `transferUserInfo` response so the round trip survives unreachability and the 90 s call runs under a phone-side background `URLSession`.
Remove the relay: let the watchOS app call the self-hosted backend directly with `URLSession` (watchOS apps route through the paired iPhone transparently when they have no WiFi/LTE of their own).
Keep both: direct call preferred, relay as fallback when the watch has no route.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Remove the relay and let the watch call the backend directly. This deletes the foreground-service hack, deletes the 30 s-vs-90 s timeout mismatch bug (documented gap #9), and deletes the whole `WearChatRelayService` class of complexity. The iPhone provisions the watch with the backend base URL and an auth token over WatchConnectivity, and the watch stores the token in its own Keychain with `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` (so it survives a locked-wrist background fetch). Keep a `transferUserInfo`-based phone relay ONLY as a fallback for the case where the watch cannot reach the backend. Port the BLE-only-mode gate verbatim, including the exact terminal copy ('AI chat needs a GlycemicGPT server — none is set up on your phone.') and its deliberate refusal to say 'try again' — and check it BEFORE showing any loading state; the watch can evaluate it locally, which also fixes documented gap 'the Chat complication does not check whether a backend is configured'. Voice input: use watchOS's system text-input controller (SwiftUI `TextField` on watchOS presents Scribble/dictation/emoji), which needs no Speech-framework entitlement and covers the dictation use case; handle its absence the way `ActivityNotFoundException` is handled today. TTS: `AVSpeechSynthesizer` with `AVSpeechSynthesisVoice.speechVoices()` for the voice-selection setting — direct port including the pre-compiled markdown-stripping regexes, the '. This is not medical advice.' suffix, and the `spokenResponseId` re-speak guard. Set a single unified timeout (adopt the phone's 90 s and show progress) rather than porting the mismatched 30/90 pair. Keep the three hardcoded quick queries.

needs_redesign.capability: Watch face configuration sync and the phone Settings > Watch UI (WatchConnectionCard, WatchFaceGalleryCard, WatchFaceConfigCard with theme/seconds/variant, WatchAppUpdateCard, WatchDataTelemetryCard)
needs_redesign.why: Roughly half of this UI controls things that do not exist on watchOS: variant selection (no custom faces), theme (Apple owns face colour), Show Seconds (Apple owns time rendering — and both of these are already inert on Android today), and 'Push watch face' / 'Check for watch update' (both impossible on iOS). What remains — reachability status, toggles that actually gate behaviour, graph overlays, glucose range, telemetry — ports, plus iOS adds new state worth surfacing that Android has no analogue for.
options: Port the UI literally and leave the dead controls in place (repeats the Android defect on a new platform).
Delete the inert controls and replace the push/update cards with a guided complication-setup flow and a version-mismatch banner.
Keep a 'theme' control but rebind it to the watch APP's own colour scheme (which IS full colour and IS under our control) rather than to the face.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Delete `cfg_theme` and `cfg_show_seconds` from the wire contract entirely rather than porting toggles that do nothing — Android's own notes confirm they have zero consumers. Rebind 'theme' to an in-app appearance/high-contrast accessibility setting for the watch app's own screens (alerts, graph detail, chat), which is genuinely meaningful. Replace WatchFaceGalleryCard with a guided 'Set up your watch face' flow: which complication families we provide, what each shows, and step-by-step instructions to add them (optionally offering a shareable `.watchface` configuration file per recommended layout — the closest Apple analogue to variant selection). Replace WatchAppUpdateCard with a version-parity banner (iOS build vs watch build) plus a link to the Watch app's install flow. Keep and extend WatchDataTelemetryCard with iOS-specific honesty state that has no Android analogue and matters a lot here: `WCSession.activationState`, `isPaired`, `isWatchAppInstalled`, `isComplicationEnabled`, `isReachable`, and `remainingComplicationUserInfoTransfers` (the remaining daily high-priority wrist-refresh budget). Keep the real toggles — Show IoB, Show Glucose Graph, Wrist Alerts, Graph Range 1H/3H/6H, and the four graph-overlay switches — and keep re-pushing config on reconnect via the monotonic-`seq` context write.

needs_redesign.capability: Wear module manifest, permissions and service registration (VIBRATE, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC, POST_NOTIFICATIONS, PUSH_WATCH_FACES, SET_PUSHED_WATCH_FACE_AS_ACTIVE, REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES, BIND_COMPLICATION_PROVIDER, standalone=false)
needs_redesign.why: Nothing maps one-to-one. iOS uses entitlements plus Info.plist usage descriptions plus capability toggles, several of the Android permissions have no iOS counterpart at all (VIBRATE, REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES, the two watch-face-push permissions), and one iOS requirement — the Critical Alerts entitlement — is gated behind a written request to Apple rather than a manifest line.
options: Enumerate an iOS entitlement/Info.plist manifest as the porting deliverable and treat the Android manifest as a checklist to retire.
Defer entitlements until the app is functional (risks discovering a Critical Alerts denial after the architecture is built around it).
needs_redesign.recommendation: Write the iOS manifest up front and file the Critical Alerts request early, because a denial changes the alerting design. Required set for this subsystem: `UIBackgroundModes` = `bluetooth-central`, `remote-notification`, `fetch`, `processing`; `BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers`; `NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription`; App Groups (one for iOS app ↔ iOS widget, a SEPARATE one for watch app ↔ watch widget — App Groups do NOT span the iPhone and the Watch, which is a common and expensive misconception); `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.time-sensitive`; `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts` (Apple-approved); `NSSupportsLiveActivities` and `NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates` if Live Activities are adopted; `WKCompanionAppBundleIdentifier` and `WKRunsIndependentlyOfCompanionApp = false` (the Android `standalone=false` analogue — the watch app depends on the phone for pump data); and, because the backend is self-hosted and may sit on a LAN, `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` + `NSBonjourServices` and a narrowly-scoped ATS exception rather than `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`. Retire VIBRATE (notifications), FOREGROUND_SERVICE* (no foreground services), REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES and both PUSH_WATCH_FACES permissions (impossible), and BIND_COMPLICATION_PROVIDER (WidgetKit needs no equivalent).

needs_redesign.capability: Installation and distribution (ADB sideload of wear-device-release.apk, optional watchface-release.apk, GitHub Releases, the documented 'most complicated step' developer-grade workflow)
needs_redesign.why: None of it applies. There is no sideloading, no ADB, no separate watch artifact to install, and no GitHub Releases distribution path for iOS. The stated plan is TestFlight, which brings its own rules: every first build of a version goes through Beta App Review before external testers get it, builds expire after 90 days, and external testing is capped at 10,000 testers.
options: TestFlight only.
TestFlight plus a documented self-build path with a free Apple developer account (the Loop/Trio model, 7-day resigning), for users who want no dependency on the project's TestFlight slot.
App Store submission (subjects the app to full review of the medical-monitoring claims).
needs_redesign.recommendation: TestFlight as the primary path, and this is a MASSIVE user-experience improvement over the Android story: the watchOS app is embedded in the iOS app bundle and installs automatically as a counterpart, so the documented 'the Wear OS install is genuinely the most complicated step' problem simply ceases to exist. Document the two things that replace it: (1) the watch app may need a manual install from the iPhone's Watch app if 'Automatic App Install' is off, and (2) complications must be added by the user to their chosen face — write that guide, because it is the new 'most complicated step'. Carry the honest doc notes forward verbatim, especially 'The watch app is read-only. No interaction with it can deliver insulin, change pump settings, or modify your data' — App Review will read this and it is also true. Add the TestFlight-specific facts to the user doc: 90-day build expiry, the need to reinstall, and that a lapsed build stops monitoring.

impossible.capability: Custom watch faces — the DIGITAL_FULL and ANALOG_MECHANICAL WFF v2 faces (450×450 circular scenes, five/three complication slots with DefaultProviderPolicy binding our own providers, DigitalClock/TimeText with AMBIENT variants, AnalogClock with drawable hands, branding text, per-variant overlay defaults)
impossible.why: watchOS provides no third-party watch face API of any kind. Apple owns the face: its layout, its clock rendering, its ambient/Always-On behaviour, its tint, and which complication slots exist. There is no WFF analogue, no way to draw a face, and no way to place branding on one. This has been true for the entire life of the platform and there is no indication it is changing. The face-level control the Android design depends on — knowing exactly which providers occupy which slots, and shipping a layout that guarantees BG, IoB, graph, alerts and chat are all visible together — is simply not available.
impossible.closest_alternative: Three things together get most of the user value. (1) WidgetKit complications in all four accessory families that the USER places on an Apple face — the data still reaches the wrist, but the layout is theirs and each complication must be added manually. (2) A shareable `.watchface` file bundled in the app: watchOS lets an app offer a watch-face configuration (an Apple face type with our complications pre-assigned to slots) that the user taps to add. That is the closest honest analogue to 'Push watch face' — it approximates the DIGITAL_FULL and ANALOG_MECHANICAL layouts using Apple's Modular/Infograph-style faces, but the user must confirm, and we control assignment, not rendering. (3) A Live Activity on the iPhone that iOS forwards into the watch Smart Stack, giving a large glanceable BG/trend/IoB/coverage surface with no user configuration at all — this is arguably a better default than a face for the first-run experience. The per-variant overlay defaults become plain user settings.

impossible.capability: Watch Face Push — phone side (WatchFacePusher: asset SHA-256 verification against BuildConfig, CapabilityClient node discovery, ChannelClient streaming, 120 s watchdog) and watch side (WatchFaceReceiveService, WatchFaceInstaller with addWatchFace/updateWatchFace/setWatchFaceAsActive, DWF validation token, the slot-limit retry, the Samsung double-update complication-rebind workaround, WatchFacePermissionActivity)
impossible.why: Two independent Apple prohibitions. First, there is no watch face installation API at all — see above; nothing on watchOS corresponds to `WatchFacePushManager`, and no app can set the active watch face. Second, even if a face format existed, App Store Review Guideline 2.5.2 forbids an app downloading, installing, or executing code that is not part of the reviewed bundle; pushing an executable artifact to a paired device is squarely within that prohibition. Neither the `SET_PUSHED_WATCH_FACE_AS_ACTIVE` permission model nor the DWF validator has any iOS counterpart.
impossible.closest_alternative: Ship the complications in the app bundle (reviewed, signed, installed with the app) and replace the push UI with a guided setup flow plus an optional in-app `.watchface` share the user confirms. The integrity guarantees the push path was buying — SHA-256 verification of the asset, the PK magic-byte check, the 50 MB cap, the validation token — are provided instead by Apple's code signing and App Review, which is a strictly stronger guarantee. The 'Success means only that bytes were transferred' gap (and the unimplemented Story 32.4 status listener) becomes moot: there is nothing to transfer.

impossible.capability: Watch APK self-update over the data link (WearAppUpdateChecker against GitHub Releases, downloadWearApk with https/host enforcement and 100 MB cap, WearApkPusher, WatchApkReceiveService, PackageInstaller session, UpdateInstallReceiver, the Idle→Checking→Available→Downloading→Pushing→Installing→Success state machine)
impossible.why: iOS has no `PackageInstaller`, no `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES`, and no sideload path. An app cannot install another app or update itself, on the phone or on the watch. App Store Review Guideline 2.5.2 explicitly prohibits downloading and executing code outside the reviewed bundle, and Guideline 3.1.1-adjacent rules prohibit alternative distribution from inside an App Store/TestFlight app. Downloading an executable artifact from GitHub Releases and installing it is not achievable by any supported means, including under the EU alternative-distribution regime (which permits alternative marketplaces, not an app installing another app).
impossible.closest_alternative: The watchOS app ships inside the iOS app bundle, so a TestFlight update of the iPhone app updates the watch app too — no separate artifact, no separate check, no separate install. This removes the entire subsystem rather than replacing it, and it removes the documented lie in it ('Success' being a bare 15-second timer rather than a confirmation). Keep only the honest remnant: an in-app banner when the installed watch app's build number does not match the iPhone app's, with a link to the Watch app so the user can trigger the counterpart install, plus an update-available prompt driven by TestFlight/App Store rather than by GitHub.

impossible.capability: Per-buildType WFF provider-package substitution and the watch-face build pipeline (GenerateWatchFaceXmlTask with the @WEAR_PKG@ hard-fail, per-variant applicationIds matching <client-app-package>.watchfacepush.<identifier>, the classes.dex strip + zipalign + v1-JAR re-sign, updateAppWatchFaceAssets, committed-assets.sha256, the enableResourceOptimizations=false guard, the EPL-1.0 xpath2 processor exclusion)
impossible.why: Moot: there is no watch face artifact to build, no WFF XML to substitute into, no DwfValidator, and no APK. The entire pipeline — including its genuinely clever safety property, that a release face can never point its complication slots at the debug wear package — exists only because Wear OS resolves complication providers by package name string at face-install time.
impossible.closest_alternative: Nothing is needed. Apple's equivalent problem does not arise: a widget extension is bound to its containing app by bundle identifier and provisioning, so a release build structurally cannot bind to a debug app's providers. Keep one artefact of the intent — a build-time assertion that the watchOS app's `WKCompanionAppBundleIdentifier`, the App Group identifiers, and the widget extension bundle IDs all agree with the containing app for the active configuration — since a mismatch there is the same silent-failure class the @WEAR_PKG@ hard-fail was protecting against. The EPL-1.0 licence exclusion protected by an instrumented test also goes away with the validator dependency.

impossible.capability: Phone-controlled watch face theme (dark / clinical_blue / high_contrast) and Show Seconds on the face
impossible.why: Apple owns watch face colour and time rendering. There is no API for an app to set a face's tint, colour scheme, or seconds display, and complications render in an accented mode using the tint the USER chose for their face. Note that both of these are already dead code on Android — the map confirms `cfg_theme` and `cfg_show_seconds` are validated, stored, and read by nothing, while the phone Settings UI still presents controls for them.
impossible.closest_alternative: Delete both from the wire contract and the settings UI rather than porting inert controls onto a second platform. Rebind the concept of 'theme' to the watch APP's own screens (alerts, graph detail, chat), which are full colour and fully under our control, and expose it as an appearance/high-contrast accessibility preference — which is genuinely valuable for a glucose app and honest about what it affects.

impossible.capability: Triggering a wrist haptic from the background without showing a notification (the GlycemicDataListenerService vibration path: waveform 0/500/200/500 for urgent, one-shot 300 ms for warning)
impossible.why: `WKInterfaceDevice.play(_:)` is only honoured while the app is running in the foreground. watchOS provides no API to vibrate the wrist from a background wake, and none to vibrate without a user-visible notification. This is a deliberate platform restriction, not an API gap.
impossible.closest_alternative: Deliver the alert as a notification scheduled on the watch (see the alert-delivery redesign), which plays the system haptic. You lose fine-grained control of the haptic waveform: `UNNotificationSound` and the interruption level determine the pattern, so the urgent-vs-warning distinction must be carried by the notification's interruption level (critical vs time-sensitive) and its sound, not by a custom vibration pattern. Note this changes an observable safety behaviour — an urgent low on Android has a distinguishable double-buzz; on watchOS the differentiator is a louder/DND-piercing critical alert, which is arguably stronger but is entitlement-dependent.

ios_requirements: The system must ship one iPhone app and one Apple Watch app from a single distributable bundle, such that installing or updating the iPhone app installs or updates the Watch app, with no separate artifact, no sideloading, and no user-performed developer workflow.

The system must let a user place GlycemicGPT complications on their chosen Apple Watch face and see, at a glance and without opening any app: current blood glucose with trend, insulin on board, a recent-glucose sparkline, an alert/coverage indicator, and an entry point to AI chat.

The system must provide guided in-app setup that tells the user exactly which complications exist, what each shows, and how to add them to their watch face — and must detect and surface the case where no complication of ours is currently on the active face.

The system must show current blood glucose on the wrist with a freshness marker: the value plain when the reading is under 6 minutes old, the value with an explicit stale marker from 6 to 15 minutes, and no value at all past 15 minutes — while continuing to show how old the reading is in every case.

The system must show insulin on board on the wrist with the same three-tier treatment on a pump policy: plain under 15 minutes, marked stale from 15 to 60 minutes, withheld past 60 minutes, never presented as current when it is not.

The system must make wrist freshness decay happen on the watch's own clock and without requiring any message from the iPhone, so that an iPhone that dies, is force-quit, or loses Bluetooth causes the wrist to degrade to 'no recent data' on schedule rather than freezing on its last reassuring value.
The system must never show a value on the wrist that is outside 20–500 mg/dL, at any freshness tier, from any source, including values restored from a local cache after a restart.

The system must convert to mmol/L for display only, using the single factor 18.0156, dividing once and rounding last, with a dot decimal separator regardless of the device locale — and must never let the display unit reach glucose validation, colour banding, threshold comparison, or plotting geometry.

The system must sanitize incoming thresholds in a dependent order that guarantees 20 ≤ urgent low ≤ low < high ≤ urgent high ≤ 500 for any input, including corrupt or hostile input, and must fall back to 70/180/55/250 when thresholds are absent.

The system must show a wrist coverage indicator that distinguishes three states — something is currently watching for lows and highs; the phone reported that nothing is watching, with the specific reason; and the phone has not reported recently — and must reserve the quiet 'all clear' presentation exclusively for the first state.

The system must encode the wrist coverage state so that it is unambiguous in monochrome and under an arbitrary user-chosen face tint, without depending on hue, because watchOS complications render in an accented mode the app does not control.

The system must render the five specific 'not watching' reasons with distinct user-facing copy — notifications denied, thresholds not synced, thresholds not configured, pump disconnected, no fresh glucose reading — and must have a distinguishable generic fallback for an unrecognised reason.

The system must have the iPhone advertise its coverage claim with an absolute expiry, and must have the watch decay that claim to 'no recent data' once the expiry passes, clamped so a corrupt or hostile expiry cannot make a dead phone appear covered for more than 30 minutes or force decay in under 10 seconds.
The system must not let the watch derive its own coverage claim; the watch renders and decays the phone's claim and never re-computes it.
The system must not persist the coverage claim across a watch app restart; after a restart, coverage must read as unknown until the phone reports again.

The system must treat a device clock that has jumped backward by more than 60 seconds as untrustworthy on both honesty axes: coverage reads unknown, feed freshness reads too-stale, and age labels say so rather than claiming 'just now'.

The system must deliver an alert to the wrist with a haptic even when the iPhone is unlocked and in active use, which requires the alert notification to be scheduled on the Watch itself rather than mirrored from the iPhone.

The system must be able to break through Silent Mode, Do Not Disturb, and Sleep Focus for urgent low and urgent high alerts, and must degrade to a Time Sensitive alert with an explicit in-app statement of the reduced guarantee if that capability is unavailable.

The system must re-alarm the wrist on a sustained alert every 30 minutes, scheduled locally on the Watch so the re-alarm continues even if the iPhone stops responding — and must terminate that ladder, with an explicit stale/not-watching notification, once the underlying reading ages past 15 minutes rather than re-alarming indefinitely off a frozen snapshot.

The system must let the user turn wrist alerts off, must state plainly in that setting that doing so disables all wrist alerting for lows and highs, and must acknowledge that the operating system and the Watch app give the user independent notification controls the app cannot override.

The system must never retract a shown alert on the basis of data it cannot vouch for: when a reading is not alertable, the alert relay must take no action at all — no send, no clear, no state change — and must let the wrist copy age out on the watch's own clock instead.
The system must refresh a still-live alert on the wrist at least every 5 minutes so that an ongoing alert never crosses the 6-minute staleness band and gets greyed out while it is still true.

The system must let the user dismiss an alert from the wrist — from the alert screen and from the notification itself — and must identify the specific alert being dismissed rather than assuming the most recent one.

The system must acknowledge a wrist dismiss locally before attempting any server call, so the dismiss is truthful even with no backend reachable, and must clear the phone-side latch so the same episode does not immediately re-alarm.

The system must show a full-screen glucose graph on the Watch with pan-back-in-time and tap-for-value, in full colour, honouring the user's basal-rate, bolus-marker, insulin-on-board and activity-mode overlay preferences.
The system must use one glucose Y-axis clamp across every graph surface, so no reading is visible on one chart and clipped off another.

The system must forward basal, bolus and insulin-on-board history for the last 6 hours to the Watch, capped at 500 records per type, and must reject at receipt any record with a basal rate above 15 U/hr, any bolus component above 25 U, a negative insulin-on-board value, or a non-positive timestamp.
The system must recover gracefully from a truncated or malformed history payload by rendering no overlay rather than crashing or rendering partial garbage.

The system must let the user ask the AI a question from the Watch by voice or text, must speak the answer aloud when the user has enabled that, must append the not-medical-advice statement to spoken output, and must offer the same three quick queries.

The system must tell the user on the Watch, before any loading state, that AI chat requires a configured GlycemicGPT server when none is set up — naming the permanent condition and where to fix it, and never suggesting a retry.
The system must use a single AI request timeout shared by the Watch and the backend call, so a late answer can never replace a displayed timeout error with a success state.

The system must cache the most recent glucose reading, glucose history, insulin on board and display unit on the Watch and restore them on a cold start, in storage readable while the Watch is locked, so a complication renders real data immediately rather than '--'.

The system must sync display and overlay preferences from the iPhone to the Watch on every change and re-sync on every reconnection, and must not offer any preference that does not change observable behaviour.

The system must show the user, in iPhone settings, the true state of the wrist link: whether a Watch is paired, whether our Watch app is installed, whether any of our complications is on the active face, whether the Watch is currently reachable, the last glucose and insulin values the Watch actually holds with their timestamps, and how much of today's high-priority wrist-refresh budget remains.

The system must budget wrist complication refreshes against the operating system's daily allowance and must pre-compute all time-driven state changes as future timeline entries, so that freshness decay and coverage expiry always occur even when no refresh budget remains.

The system must show a glanceable glucose surface on the iPhone Lock Screen and Dynamic Island that also appears in the Watch Smart Stack without the user configuring anything, and must carry the same freshness and coverage honesty as the complications.

The system must carry full-colour glucose banding — red at or beyond urgent thresholds, amber at or beyond warning thresholds, green in range, with warning boundaries inclusive — on every surface where the operating system permits full colour, and must convey the same information without hue on every surface where it does not.

The system must be developable and demonstrable end to end in the iOS and watchOS Simulators using an injectable simulated glucose and pump-history source, because Core Bluetooth is entirely unavailable in the Simulator and no real pump data can reach the app there.
The system must state plainly, in the user documentation and in the app, that the Watch experience is read-only: no interaction with it can deliver insulin, change a pump setting, or modify data.
The system must warn the user when the installed Watch app build does not match the iPhone app build, and must not attempt to update the Watch app itself.

The system must share every safety-critical constant and pure decision function — the 20–500 bound, 18.0156, threshold sanitization, the freshness tiers, the 60-second backward-clock guard, colour banding, the coverage decision, and the alert relay state machine — as one compiled module linked by the iPhone app, the Watch app, and both widget extensions, with tests pinning every documented boundary pair and the cross-surface mmol/L fixture.

The system must expose the same accessibility descriptions on every wrist surface that the Android complications expose today, including the stale-alert, not-watching and no-recent-data phrasings, since screen-reader output is the one channel where the exact copy survives unchanged.

risks.risk: The Critical Alerts entitlement (`com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts`) is granted by Apple case-by-case on a written request, not by ticking a capability. Without it, no notification from this app can break through Silent Mode, Do Not Disturb or Sleep Focus. That deletes the overnight urgent-low alert — the single highest-consequence behaviour in the product — for any user with a Focus enabled, which is most users while sleeping. Android has no equivalent gate: the wear service vibrates directly.
risks.mitigation: File the request at the start of the project, not at the end, with the medical justification and the read-only-monitoring framing (which is a materially easier case than a closed-loop app). Design the alerting layer so the interruption level is a single configuration point that can degrade from `.critical` to `.timeSensitive` without restructuring. If denied, the app must say so explicitly in the alert settings screen — 'this app cannot alert you through Do Not Disturb' is exactly the kind of coverage honesty the GLY-116 architecture already exists to enforce, and hiding it would be the same class of lie the whole subsystem is designed to prevent.

risks.risk: The wrist complication refresh budget is metered and small relative to a 5-minute CGM cadence. `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` draws from a system daily allowance (historically around 50), and WidgetKit reload requests are separately budgeted. 288 readings per day cannot each buy a wrist refresh. If the design assumes push-per-reading, the complication will appear to work in development and then silently stop updating on real devices partway through the day.
risks.mitigation: Make timeline pre-computation the primary mechanism, not an optimisation: every freshness transition and every coverage expiry is a future timeline entry that costs nothing. Spend metered transfers only on band crossings, alert changes, coverage changes and a ~15-minute floor. Instrument `WCSession.remainingComplicationUserInfoTransfers` and surface it in the Settings > Watch telemetry card so exhaustion is visible rather than mysterious. Note explicitly that the Simulator does NOT enforce these budgets — this defect is undiscoverable without on-device soak testing.

risks.risk: watchOS complications render in an accented/tinted mode. The alerts bell encodes its entire six-branch coverage-honesty decision in hue (grey / amber / red), and the graph encodes basal, bolus, activity-mode and glucose banding entirely in hue. A literal port produces complications where 'everything is fine' and 'your phone is dead and nothing is watching' are visually identical.
risks.mitigation: Re-encode on symbol, shape and text before writing any of the complication views, and add a merge gate: greyscale screenshots of all six alert-bell branches must be distinguishable by a reviewer who has not read the code. Keep the accessibility labels verbatim from the Android descriptions — they already carry the full state and are the one channel that survives intact.

risks.risk: There is no reliable periodic wake on iOS. The 3-minute coverage heartbeat — explicitly documented as the dead-phone detector, and load-bearing enough that the `_ts` dedup-buster exists solely to make it deliverable — cannot be reproduced as a timer. A naive port produces a wrist that falsely decays to 'no recent data' on a healthy phone, which trains the user to ignore the cue, which is worse than not having it.
risks.mitigation: Change the wire contract from cadence-based to deadline-based: the phone advertises an absolute validity expiry and the watch decays against that, so irregular delivery no longer causes false decay. Piggyback the claim on every Core Bluetooth wake, which is the same event stream that proves the phone is alive. Validate on device across a full sleep cycle with the phone in Low Power Mode, because this failure mode is invisible in the Simulator, which does not suspend apps.

risks.risk: A force-quit iPhone app is never relaunched by Core Bluetooth state restoration until the user reopens it. The pump link, the alert relay and the coverage claim all stop with no notification and no recovery. This has no Android equivalent — a foreground service survives the app switcher.
risks.mitigation: This is unfixable and must be handled by honesty, not engineering. The existing two-axis design already produces the correct behaviour (the wrist decays to 'no recent data'), so the requirement is (a) never weaken that decay, (b) name force-quit explicitly in the user documentation and in the in-app degraded-state copy, and (c) consider a low-frequency background-refresh task whose only job is to notice it was not running and tell the user.

risks.risk: Core Bluetooth is entirely unavailable in the iOS Simulator (`CBCentralManager` reports unsupported), so no real pump or CGM data can reach the app during the developer's stated Simulator-based loop. Every downstream behaviour in this subsystem — the alert relay state machine, freshness decay, coverage claims, history overlays, the complications — is fed by that data.
risks.mitigation: Build a first-class injectable data source behind the same interface the real driver implements, with scripted scenarios (a low crossing, a sustained urgent low, a CGM dropout at exactly the 6- and 15-minute boundaries, a phone-death simulation, a backward clock jump). This is not a test convenience — it is the only way to exercise this subsystem before hardware, and it also becomes the demo and the regression harness. Ship it behind a debug build configuration.

risks.risk: Several other capabilities in this subsystem are also unverifiable in the Simulator: haptics are a no-op in the Watch Simulator so no alert can actually be felt; the physical Silent switch and real Focus modes do not exist, so critical-alert breakthrough cannot be validated; complication reload budgets and `transferCurrentComplicationUserInfo` limits are not enforced; watch face sharing (`.watchface`) is device-only; background refresh scheduling and budgets do not reflect device behaviour; the Simulator Keychain is not Secure-Enclave-backed and Data Protection classes are not truly enforced, so the 'complication renders while the watch is locked' path cannot be proven; and HealthKit is unavailable on the watchOS Simulator entirely.
risks.mitigation: Accept the Simulator for layout, state-machine, formatting and timeline-logic work, and define an explicit on-device acceptance checklist for exactly these items: felt haptic for each alert tier, breakthrough with Sleep Focus on, complication still updating after 18 hours of continuous use, complication rendering correctly after a wrist-off/lock cycle, and the `.watchface` add flow. Budget device time from the start rather than discovering the list late.

risks.risk: WatchConnectivity pairing depends on `WKCompanionAppBundleIdentifier` matching the containing app. A mismatch produces a watch app that installs and launches but whose session never activates — the exact silent-failure signature of the Android applicationId bug discovered in Story 32.8, where the watch kept rendering its last reassuring values with no error surfaced.
risks.mitigation: Assert the relationship at build time (a script phase comparing the bundle identifiers, App Group identifiers and widget extension IDs across all targets for the active configuration), and surface `WCSession.activationState` prominently in the Settings > Watch telemetry card so the failure is visible in seconds rather than after a debugging session.

risks.risk: The self-hosted backend will frequently live on a LAN address or a self-signed host. iOS requires `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` plus declared Bonjour services for local network access, and App Transport Security blocks plaintext HTTP; a blanket `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads` draws App Review scrutiny. This bites the watch directly if the Watch app calls the backend itself for AI chat and background fetch.
risks.mitigation: Support HTTPS with a user-supplied or pinned certificate as the primary path, add narrowly-scoped ATS exceptions rather than a blanket one, and request local-network permission with a clear purpose string on first backend configuration. Make the backend-optional local mode a genuinely first-class path so a user who cannot get networking right still gets pump monitoring, alerting and the full wrist experience minus AI chat — which is exactly the posture the existing BLE-only-mode terminal copy already takes.

risks.risk: The AI chat feature will be read by App Review as health advice delivered by a model. Guideline 1.4.1 and the medical-app provisions require accuracy and appropriate disclaimers, and the app's overall framing as glucose monitoring invites scrutiny of whether it makes diagnostic or therapeutic claims.
risks.mitigation: Keep the existing disclaimer behaviour unchanged and make it non-dismissible: the backend disclaimer when present, the 'Not medical advice. Consult your doctor.' default when blank, and the spoken '. This is not medical advice.' suffix. Lead the review notes with the read-only architecture — no bolus, no basal change, no pump-setting modification, ever — which is the strongest single fact in the submission.

risks.risk: TestFlight builds expire after 90 days and external testing is capped at 10,000 testers. For an app people rely on for overnight low alerts, an expired build is a silent monitoring outage.
risks.mitigation: Warn in-app well before expiry with a countdown once inside 14 days, state the expiry in the onboarding, and maintain a release cadence that never lets a build reach expiry. Document a self-build path for users who do not want the dependency.

risks.risk: Removing the phone chat relay in favour of a direct Watch-to-backend call puts a backend auth token in the Watch's Keychain. A Watch is more easily lost than a phone and its Keychain has a different threat profile.
risks.mitigation: Store the token with `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` (never `WhenUnlocked`, which would break the locked-wrist background fetch, and never a synchronizable class), scope it to a read-only credential where the backend supports it, provision it only over an active WatchConnectivity session, and clear it when the user signs out on the phone. Keep the phone relay as the fallback so a user who declines to provision the Watch still gets chat.

risks.risk: Porting the two Android surfaces that have no freshness de-emphasis at all — the sparkline complication and the full-screen graph detail — carries the defect onto a platform where the wrist is even more likely to be looked at in isolation from the phone. A three-hour-old chart currently renders identically to a live one.
risks.mitigation: Fix during the port rather than after: apply the same three-tier treatment to both graph surfaces (de-emphasise the trace and label the window explicitly once the newest reading is stale, withhold the trace entirely past too-stale), and unify the two conflicting Y clamps. Both are one-line changes in the shared module and both are cheaper now than as a later regression.

risks.risk: The Android watch app never receives install/update status back (documented gap #1: status messages are write-only, `Success` is a bare 15-second timer). The iOS port removes the artifacts that path served, but the same class of defect can reappear in the new bridge — for example, showing 'synced to watch' when a transfer was merely enqueued.
risks.mitigation: Make every wrist-state claim in the iPhone UI derive from something the Watch actually acknowledged — the `WCSessionDelegate` transfer-finished callback and the telemetry read-back of what the Watch currently holds — and never from 'we called the API'. The existing telemetry card already reads values back; extend that principle to every sync affordance.

questions_for_pm: Will the project apply to Apple for the Critical Alerts entitlement, and under what legal entity? Apple grants it only by written request with a medical justification tied to a developer account, which for an open-source project with no company is a governance decision this repo cannot answer. It is decision-shaping rather than cosmetic: with the entitlement, urgent low and urgent high alerts reach the wrist through Silent Mode, Do Not Disturb and Sleep Focus, matching what the Android watch does today by vibrating directly; without it, the app can only use Time Sensitive alerts, overnight urgent-low alerting is not guaranteed, and the app must say so plainly to the user. The alerting layer should be built so the interruption level is a single swappable configuration either way, but whether to file, and whether to ship if denied, is a product and risk call.
